lesson.title: When a Curve Has No Well-Defined Slope
lesson.summary: Defines a differentiable function as one whose derivative limit exists at every point, and proves with one-sided limits that the absolute value function fails this test at its corner.
lesson.body:
Every derivative computation so far has assumed, often without saying so, that the limit in the definition actually exists. A function for which f prime of a exists is called differentiable at a, and a function that is differentiable at every point in its domain is simply called a differentiable function. This is not automatic. Some functions have points where the defining limit fails to exist, and at those points there is no tangent line and no derivative, however hard you look.

The classic example is the absolute value function, f(x) = the absolute value of x, at the point x = 0. Everywhere except at 0 this function is perfectly smooth, its graph is just two straight rays, but at 0 the two rays meet at a sharp corner, and that corner is where differentiability breaks down. Check this directly with the limit definition: f prime of 0 would be the limit as h approaches 0 of [absolute value of (0 + h) minus absolute value of 0] divided by h, which simplifies to the limit of absolute value of h divided by h.

This limit has to be examined from both sides separately, because the absolute value function behaves differently depending on the sign of h. For h approaching 0 from the positive side, h is positive, so absolute value of h equals h, and the ratio h divided by h equals 1 for every such h, so the right hand limit is 1. For h approaching 0 from the negative side, h is negative, so absolute value of h equals negative h, and the ratio becomes negative h divided by h, which equals negative 1 for every such h, so the left hand limit is negative 1. Since the limit from the right, 1, does not equal the limit from the left, negative 1, the two sided limit does not exist. Therefore f prime of 0 does not exist, and the absolute value function is not differentiable at x = 0, even though it is perfectly well defined and continuous there.

Geometrically this matches intuition exactly: near a sharp corner there is no single line that both touches the curve and matches its direction, because the direction itself jumps abruptly from a slope of negative 1 on the left to a slope of positive 1 on the right. Away from that one point, however, the absolute value function is differentiable everywhere, with derivative equal to negative 1 for all negative x and positive 1 for all positive x.

By contrast, polynomial functions like x squared and x cubed, both differentiated earlier by the same limit definition, are differentiable at every real number. In each case the h in the denominator canceled out through ordinary algebra, leaving an expression with no h left in it before the limit was ever taken, so the limit existed at every input without exception. That clean cancellation is exactly what fails for the absolute value function at x = 0, where no amount of algebra removes the dependence on the sign of h before the limit is evaluated.

This example matters beyond its own graph because it shows that differentiability is a genuinely stronger requirement than just having a defined function value. Being defined at a point, or even being continuous there, is not enough to guarantee a derivative exists; the two one sided versions of the difference quotient limit must agree. The next sections build on exactly this distinction.
